headline: 168 feet on the meter: cod holding tight to the gravel, bluefin finally pinning bait on top
subhead: Haddock are stacked on the mud in the Basin, and the first real tuna push of the summer showed up chasing mackerel over the northern edge.
body_markdown:
168 feet on the meter, marks stacked right on the break where the gravel gives way to hard bottom on the northwest corner of the Bank — that's where I found my cod Tuesday morning, and that's where I've been finding them most mornings this month. This time of year the fish crowd the edges where the current sweeps clean gravel, not the flat mud in the middle. Clam and herring combos on a standard cod rig, 6 to 10 ounces depending on the drift, and you want the boat moving just enough to keep the baits ticking bottom without dragging into the rocks. We've had keeper cod to 14 pounds, mixed with a lot of shorts that go back over the rail. Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers, but steady enough that if you fish three or four drifts on that edge you'll put fish in the box.

Haddock have been the better story. Stellwagen Basin, 190 to 210 feet of water, soft mud bottom — that's classic haddock structure and they've been sitting on it thick. Clam bait on a simple bottom rig outfishes jigs down there right now; the haddock are feeding tight to bottom and don't seem interested in chasing anything that moves fast. Limits haven't been automatic but a lot of boats are coming in with eight, ten, twelve fish in the 2-to-4-pound range, a few pushing 6. The mud holds its structure better than the gravel edges when the tide runs hard, so on the bigger tide swings this week that's where I've been sending people. Watch your drift speed — over the mud you want to be almost stationary, and if the current's ripping you're better off waiting for the tide change than fighting it.

Now the tuna. This is the part of the report I've been waiting to write. Mackerel have piled onto the Bank in real numbers over the last ten days, and where you get that much bait balled up on top, the bluefin show up to work it. We've had fish breaking on the surface over the northern part of Stellwagen and out toward Tillies Bank, mostly in that 100-to-160-foot range, chasing mackerel schools that are thick enough to turn the water black on the sounder. Trolling green machines and small spreader bars in the 6-to-8 knot range has raised fish, but the better bite has come from live-lining mackerel right into the melee once you spot birds working and fish showing on top. These aren't giants yet — mostly fish in the 60-to-150-pound class from what I've seen boated and what other captains are reporting at the dock — but that class of fish eats aggressively and gives you a real fight on standup gear. A couple boats have connected on bigger fish north of Tillies, closer to 200, but that's not the bulk of what's around.

The pattern makes sense if you think about what's happening with the bait. Mackerel schools have been moving up onto the Bank chasing the same current edges and thermoclines that push everything else around out here, and the stripers working the South Shore beaches this past week were feeding on the same push of mackerel closer to the beach. When bait stacks up like this in mid-July, it's rarely one species benefiting — you get bass working the inshore edge of the school and tuna working the offshore edge, sometimes within a few miles of each other. That's exactly what's been happening.

Conditions have been workable but not flat calm — a light chop most mornings, laying down by midday, which has made the surface bite easier to spot once the wind eases. I haven't seen anything that looks like a hard thermal break setting up on the Bank yet this week, which tells me the tuna showing now are opportunistic fish riding the bait rather than a school that's locked in and staying put. That can change fast. If the mackerel hold their position over the next few days, I'd expect the tuna numbers to build rather than fade — this early in the season, more fish tend to filter onto the Bank once word gets out among the school that there's food up there, so to speak.

For the week ahead: I'd keep working the gravel edge on the northwest corner for cod first thing, before the tide picks up too much, then slide into the Basin for haddock on the last of the ebb when the mud settles down. If you've got a tuna rod rigged, don't leave it in the rack — glass the surface on the ride out and ride in, because the bite has been coming in short, violent windows when the mackerel get pushed up and the tuna crash through them. Best case, this bait stays put through the weekend and the tuna action builds into something more consistent. If the mackerel push off the Bank the way they sometimes do with a wind shift, I'd expect the tuna to follow them east toward Tillies, and that's where I'd go looking next.
